column3: The annunciation explicitly identifies the promised Messiah as Jesus, son of Mary, establishing the identity asserted in the focus ayah.
Its judgment of people over what they disputed gives only a general parallel to the focus ayah's disputed truth.
Its instruction to speak rightly about vulnerable descendants does not clarify Jesus's identity or the dispute about him.
It again names Jesus son of Mary and describes conflicting, uncertain claims about him, directly paralleling the focus ayah's truth claim.
Jesus's preceding declaration of peace over his birth, death, and resurrection continues the infant speech whose identity statement follows.
It contrasts merely spoken claims of filiation with God's truthful speech, a useful analogue to the rejection of false divine sonship.
Jesus, son of Mary, speaks in prayer here, providing a later portrayal of the person identified in the focus ayah.
The next ayah explicitly rejects divine offspring and explains creation by command, giving the immediate theological resolution of the focus claim.
God's declaration that He speaks the truth provides a compact theological parallel to the focus's "word of truth."
It portrays a matter long disputed as finally brought before those disputing it, a general pattern behind the focus ayah.
This local warning about the settled matter and unbelief extends the same narrative section after the contested identity has been stated.
Moses's commitment to say only truth about God is a broad prophetic parallel to the focus ayah's true statement about Jesus.

The bare identification of Jesus son of Mary offers a limited identity parallel without addressing the disputed claim.

The affirmation that truth comes from God and the command not to be among disputers directly supports the focus ayah's truth-versus-dispute framing.

The oath concerning the construction of the sky has no relevant connection to Jesus or contested filiation.

Its critique of assigning children to God is a relevant but less specific analogue to the correction following the focus ayah.

The later claim that the Merciful has taken a child is the false filiation the focus ayah and its continuation reject.

The description of people in conflicting speech broadly parallels rival claims against the focus ayah's truth.

The local assertion that the Merciful has taken a child is the false claim answered by the immediate context of the focus ayah.
Jesus, son of Mary, identifies himself as God's messenger and faces rejection of clear proofs, closely confirming his proper status.
The fulfillment of God's word on the condemned is only a remote parallel to the focus's word of truth.

Recognition of revelation like recognition of sons does not clarify the truth about Jesus.
The triumph of the religion of truth is too general to explain the focus claim.
The messenger's announcement of a pure boy to Mary supplies the immediate origin narrative for the Jesus named in the focus ayah.

Its command to avoid false speech gives a general ethical contrast to the focus ayah's word of truth.

Moses's declaration that he is a messenger from the Lord offers a general prophetic identity parallel.
The signs in night and day do not clarify Jesus's identity or the dispute about him.

Lot's reference to his daughters does not clarify the disputed truth concerning Jesus.

Doubt about meeting God is a remote lexical parallel to the focus ayah's description of disputers.
The reminder of ordinary human creation does not clarify Jesus's exceptional identity.

Mary points her accusers to the infant, directly introducing the speech that reaches the focus ayah.
Abraham's prayer for his descendants against idolatry does not clarify the identity of Jesus.

Mary's appeal for protection frames the threatened innocence and public vulnerability answered by the infant's true testimony.
Mary's denial of human contact establishes the virginal conception underlying the contested identity of Jesus.
Mary's conception of Jesus and withdrawal with him supplies the direct narrative bridge to his later public identification.
Mary's labor portrays the human birth circumstance that the focus ayah names without making it divine filiation.

Mary's commanded silence prepares the decisive transfer of testimony to the infant Jesus.
Jesus's declaration of servitude, scripture, prophethood, blessing, prayer, and almsgiving is part of the same speech that culminates in the focus ayah.
The section's conclusion that God inherits earth and all upon it frames the ultimate judgment of the rival claims just described.
The near-collapse of heaven and earth over the claim that the Merciful has taken a child intensifies the false filiation rejected after the focus ayah.
Its statement that every being comes to the Merciful as a servant reinforces Jesus's self-identification as God's servant.
God's complete enumeration of creation gives only broad support to the surrounding assertion of divine sovereignty.
Each creature's solitary return to God supports the surrounding denial that any creature stands as a divine child.
The gift of clear proofs and the Holy Spirit to Jesus son of Mary directly confirms his prophetic, not divine, status.
The claim that God has taken a son is explicitly rejected, directly paralleling the correction in the focus ayah's immediate continuation.
Jesus son of Mary is distinguished by clear proofs and the Holy Spirit, offering a direct Quranic account of his special prophetic role.
Mary's conception is explained through God's creative command, directly grounding the identity asserted in the focus ayah.
Jesus's signs to the Children of Israel establish his God-given mission and help define the true status under dispute.
The comparison of Jesus with Adam directly rejects an inference from extraordinary creation to divine sonship.
The disciples' response to Jesus records an early communal reception of his mission, relevant to later factional disagreement about him.
The grave accusation against Mary supplies the slander that the birth narrative and Jesus's speech publicly answer.
It treats belief in Jesus among the People of the Book as an eschatological issue, extending the question of his recognized identity.
The Messiah's refusal to disdain being God's servant directly confirms the servant status that excludes divine sonship.
It explicitly rejects the claim that God is the Messiah son of Mary, making it a direct doctrinal neighbour of the focus ayah.
It identifies Jesus son of Mary as a messenger given the Gospel, directly clarifying the identity at issue.
God's address recounts the signs given to Jesus son of Mary and anchors those signs in divine permission rather than divinity.
The disciples' belief in God and His messenger Jesus supplies a concise early confession of Jesus's messenger status.
Jesus says that he taught only worship of God, his Lord and their Lord, directly delimiting the true teaching disputed about him.
Jesus's inclusion among prophets gives broad support to his prophetic status without addressing the contested claim.
The denial that God could have a child without a consort gives a direct theological rebuttal to false divine filiation.

The assertion that God has taken a child is rejected as speech without knowledge, closely paralleling the focus's truth against disputation.
